info.bio: Body Count es una banda de rap metal estadounidense formada en Los Ángeles, California en 1990. Fue fundada por Ice-T, conocido por sus contribuciones en el hip hop. Ice-T fundó el grupo debido a su interés por el heavy metal, y asumió el papel de vocalista, escribiendo las letras de la mayoría de las canciones, mientras que la música fue escrita por el guitarrista Ernie C. Su álbum debut llamado Body Count fue lanzado por Sire Records en 1992.

scenes.name: Ice-T y el reality rap de Los Ángeles
scenes.book: The Come Up: An Oral History of the Rise of Hip-Hop
scenes.author: Jonathan Abrams
scenes.desc: Del electro de Radiotron, Ice-T (lector de Iceberg Slim, exmilitar, amigo de Afrika Islam, que lo llevó a Nueva York con Melle Mel y Caz) tomó de «P.S.K.» la entrega relajada: «6 ’N the Mornin’» (1986), cara B de «Dog ’N the Wax», con el 808 de Afrika Islam y DJ Unknown, contaba en primera persona la redada de las seis de la mañana, la cárcel, Crenshaw: bajó las pulsaciones del baile a la música para el coche de los lowriders. Rhyme Pays (Sire, 1987): Seymour Stein dudó y Ice le dijo «quizá eso que sientes es dinero»; nunca volvió a cuestionarle, ni con «Cop Killer». KDAY tuvo que retirarla por las quejas de C. Delores Tucker. Por la misma época, Toddy Tee vendía desde su coche «Batterram» (1985), sobre el ariete de la policía, y Mixmaster Spade era el dios de los buscavidas (Above the Law). Ice-T siempre contó las consecuencias: lo llamó reality rap.

scenes.name: 1992: Cop Killer, Sister Souljah y la censura de Time Warner
scenes.book: The Come Up: An Oral History of the Rise of Hip-Hop
scenes.author: Jonathan Abrams
scenes.desc: Tras los disturbios de Los Ángeles, el hip hop chocó con los políticos y los intereses corporativos. Bill Clinton, con Al Gore (marido de Tipper) de compañero, condenó una frase sacada de contexto de la activista Sister Souljah, cercana a Public Enemy: el «momento Sister Souljah». La policía pidió boicotear a Time Warner por «Cop Killer» de Body Count, el grupo de heavy metal de Ice-T, aunque no era hip hop: en la junta de accionistas de julio de 1992 Charlton Heston, en nombre de la NRA, leyó en voz alta «KKK Bitch»; el consejero delegado Gerald Levin solo invocó la Primera Enmienda. Ice-T retiró la canción por las amenazas a empleados y Warner empezó a filtrar letras y portadas: no distribuyó Live and Let Die de Kool G Rap & DJ Polo y bloqueó Sleeping with the Enemy de Paris («Bush Killa»), cuya portada filtró una ayudante de Tommy Boy de familia de policías. Ice-T se marchó por la portada de Home Invasion; a Paris lo despidieron el mismo día que a Ice-T y a G Rap, cobró cien mil dólares y sus másteres y fundó Scarface Records: seis dólares y medio por disco en vez de cincuenta céntimos.

scenes.name: Black rock
scenes.book: Funk: The Music, the People, and the Rhythm of the One
scenes.author: Rickey Vincent
scenes.desc: «El funk es blues acelerado» (Clinton). Pese a Chuck Berry, Little Richard o Bo Diddley, el rock se volvió una forma blanca y la invasión británica reforzó el mito, aunque sus grupos venían del blues negro. Hendrix y Sly lo desmontaron a finales de los sesenta, pero la industria resegregó el rock en pocos años, hasta Prince. El blues eléctrico (Muddy Waters, con su «gran caída tras el golpe del tambor») tuvo su revival ante el público blanco. En la Costa Oeste, multirracial y lejos de los problemas del Norte y del Sur, florecieron bandas mestizas (Sly, Tower of Power, Santana): la influencia del rock psicodélico convirtió el funk de un R&B salvaje en algo universal. A mediados de los setenta el black rock se convirtió en funk, porque la radio obligó a quitar los solos de guitarra; solo algunos resistieron («Who Says a Funk Band Can’t Play Rock?!» de Funkadelic, Slave, Mother’s Finest, los Isley) hasta Prince y la Black Rock Coalition de Vernon Reid (1985), y en los noventa Living Colour, Body Count, Bad Brains o Fishbone.
scenes.family: Funk psicodélico y black rock: Sly, Hendrix

scenes.name: Rapcore y New Metal
scenes.book: Heavy Metal: The Music and Its Culture
scenes.author: Deena Weinstein
scenes.desc: Body Count, el grupo del rapero Ice-T, abre el rapcore con temas atractivos para chicos de todas las razas; a finales de la década las voces rapeadas se ponen de moda, aunque pocos de esos grupos son metal. Spin dedica en agosto de 1998 un reportaje al «New Metal» (Korn, Limp Bizkit con su DJ fijo), un híbrido que bebe tanto del rock alternativo, el hip-hop y el hardcore del skate californiano como de Black Sabbath y Slayer, y Rolling Stone lleva en febrero de 1999 a Rob Zombie en portada con los «10 mejores grupos de metal». Weinstein se pregunta por qué se llama metal a lo que sus músicos no quieren que se llame así: la etiqueta da una imagen más blanca y más rock, y su uso promiscuo es a la vez prueba y causa del regreso del metal. ¿Es metal Rage Against the Machine? ¿Y Sevendust o Limp Bizkit?
scenes.family: Cruces: rap, funk, industrial, grunge y nu metal

podcast.title: Ice-T's Metal Band (1989)
podcast.body: Body Count was formed around 1989 by Ice-T, primarily known as a gangster rapper, and guitarist Ernie C. They gathered high school friends in Los Angeles to create a metal band, inspired by Living Color. "They also inspired this next band, Body Count. This is Ice Tea's band. Around 1989, he got to talking to his buddy, guitarist Ernie C., and they thought it would be really cool if they formed a metal band on the side."

podcast.title: Lollapalooza 1991 Performer
podcast.body: Body Count, featuring Ice-T, was one of the bands on the first-ever Lollapalooza tour in 1991. Their inclusion highlighted the festival's genre-bending approach, which integrated alternative rock with hardcore rap and metal. "Ice Tea and Body Count, one of the bands in the first ever Lola Palusa tour in 1991."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Lollapalooza 1991 Performer
podcast.body: Ice-T & Body Count were part of the lineup for the first Lollapalooza tour in the summer of 1991, a tour that, despite initial ticket sales challenges, convinced promoters to continue the festival due to its success in drawing crowds of 20,000 people. "Along with founding band Jane's addiction, the line up included Suzy and the band sheets, living color, iced tea and body count, butthole surfers, Rawens band and some weirdo group that was never going to go anywhere called Nine-inch Nails."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Lollapalooza Performance (1991)
podcast.body: Body Counts was among the bands performing at the first Lollapalooza festival, an initiative to bring the alternative music scene to a wider audience in America. "It featured Jane's Addiction as the headliners along with up and coming bands like Nine Inch Nails and the Rollins Band along with Ice Tea and Body Counts and the Butthole Surfers and Suzy and the Banshees and more."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: "Cop Killer" Controversy (1992)
podcast.body: The song "Cop Killer" became highly controversial, widely perceived as an attack on police forces, escalating into a significant First Amendment debate in the U.S. and drawing parallels to the Black Lives Matter movement. "And there were provocations like the song Cop Killer, which was taken as an an attack on police forces everywhere. Metal thing blew up into a big first amendment debate in the US, which had many of the same elements as the Black Lives Matter movement."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: "Rock Band with a Rap Mentality"
podcast.body: Ice-T described Body Count as "a rock band with a rap mentality," reflecting their blend of heavy metal sound with lyrical themes typical of hip-hop. "Hey, Ice Tea would say, we're a rock band with a rap mentality."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: "Selling Out" Accusations from Black Audiences
podcast.body: Ice-T faced accusations of "selling out" from his black gangster rap audience for moving into the rock genre with Body Count. "First of all, Ice Tea's black audiences accused him of selling out by going in a rock direction."

podcast.title: Alternative Club and Radio Presence
podcast.body: Body Count's music was increasingly heard in alternative dance clubs and on new rock radio stations, indicating its growing crossover appeal. "Meanwhile, groups like House of Pain and Cypress Hill and Body Count were heard more and more in alternative dance clubs and on new rock radio stations."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Bridging Audiences
podcast.body: Body Count was credited with introducing hip-hop to white audiences and metal to black audiences, expanding the reach of both genres. "This brought hip-hop to white audiences and metal to black ones."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Contribution to Nu-Metal
podcast.body: Despite controversies, Body Count persevered and played a significant role in the emergence of the nu-metal movement during the mid to late 1990s, influencing bands like KoRn, Slipknot, and Limp Bizkit. "But the band continued, and they were a big part of the move into new metal in the middle in late 90s. So basically, you can draw a line from Body Count, right through corn, slipknot, and limp biscuit."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Live Performance Blend
podcast.body: Typically, during their live performances, half of the set featured Body Count's material, and the other half was dedicated to hip-hop, bridging these genres for diverse audiences. "Typically, when they played, half of the set was devoted to Body Count material, and the other was hip-hop."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Lyrical Themes
podcast.body: The band focused on issues such as racism, police brutality, inner-city crime, and various political topics in their lyrics. "And that meant focusing on things like racism, police brutality, inner city crime, and various political issues."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Reaching White Audiences
podcast.body: Body Count was instrumental in helping rap and hip hop reach more white kids, bridging cultural divides. "And thanks to groups like Body Count, Living Color, the Beastie Boys and Rage Against the Machine, rap and hip hop was able to reach both more white kids."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Warner Brothers Records Shareholder Threat
podcast.body: The controversy surrounding "Cop Killer" was so intense that shareholders threatened to withdraw all their money from Warner Brothers Records if the label did not take action regarding Body Count. "It got so crazy that shareholders threatened to pull all their money for Warner Brothers records if the label didn't do something about Body Count."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: White Audiences' Reception
podcast.body: Body Count, as an all-black metal band, did not always receive appreciation from white audiences, highlighting racial tensions in the metal scene. "And second, white audiences didn't always appreciate an all-black metal band."

xref.body: Before forming Body Count, Ice-T was primarily known as a prominent gangster rapper but also had a personal affinity for rock music, including bands like Led Zeppelin, Black Sabbath, and Judas Priest, as well as thrash metal, with Slayer being a favorite.
